name: Where On Earth
subject: Geography
tagline: Twenty questions about the map, from capitals everyone gets wrong to the driest place there is. Starts easy, ends hard.

questions.q: What is the capital of Australia?
questions.w: Canberra. Sydney and Melbourne both wanted the honour, so a new city was built between them.
questions.more: The rivalry was settled in 1908 by choosing farmland roughly halfway along the coast between the two. An American architect, Walter Burley Griffin, won the competition to design it, and the city was formally named in 1913.

questions.q: Which ocean lies between Africa and Australia?
questions.w: The Indian Ocean, the third largest, bounded by Africa, Asia, Australia and the Southern Ocean.
questions.more: It is the warmest of the oceans, which weakens its ability to absorb carbon dioxide. Its monsoon winds reverse twice a year, and sailors used that rhythm for trade between Africa, Arabia and India for well over a thousand years.

questions.q: Mount Everest sits on the border between Nepal and which other country?
questions.w: China. The northern side lies in Tibet, where the mountain is called Chomolungma.
questions.more: Climbers approach from Nepal in the south or Tibet in the north. The summit was first reached in 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay, and the mountain still grows a few millimetres a year as India pushes into Asia.

questions.q: Which is the largest country in the world by land area?
questions.w: Russia, at about 17 million square kilometres, roughly twice the size of the next largest.
questions.more: It spans eleven time zones and borders fourteen countries. Travelling the Trans-Siberian railway from Moscow to Vladivostok takes about a week without leaving the country.

questions.q: The Sahara Desert covers much of which continent?
questions.w: Africa. The Sahara stretches across the north of the continent, about the size of the United States.
questions.more: It was green as recently as six thousand years ago, with lakes and grassland, and rock paintings there show people swimming. A slow wobble in Earth's orbit shifted the monsoon south and dried it out.

questions.q: Which American state is the largest by area?
questions.w: Alaska, more than twice the size of Texas.
questions.more: The United States bought it from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million, about two cents an acre. The press mocked the deal as Seward's Folly until gold and later oil were found.

questions.q: True or false: the Equator passes through Brazil.
questions.w: True. It crosses the north of the country, near the mouth of the Amazon.
questions.more: Thirteen countries sit on the Equator. Brazil, Colombia and Indonesia are the largest, and the line also crosses Ecuador, which was named after it.

questions.q: Istanbul straddles two continents. Which two?
questions.w: Europe and Asia, split by the Bosphorus strait.
questions.more: It is the only large city on two continents, and commuters cross between them daily by ferry, bridge or the Marmaray rail tunnel under the strait. The city has been called Byzantium and Constantinople before Istanbul.

questions.q: Which country is completely surrounded by South Africa?
questions.w: Lesotho, one of only three countries in the world entirely enclosed by a single other country.
questions.more: The other two are San Marino and Vatican City, both inside Italy. Lesotho is also the only country whose entire territory sits above 1,000 metres, which is why it gets snow.

questions.q: Lake Baikal, the deepest lake on Earth, is in which country?
questions.w: Russia, in southern Siberia. It is over 1,600 metres deep.
questions.more: It holds about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet, more than all five North American Great Lakes combined. It is also ancient, around 25 million years old, and home to the nerpa, the world's only freshwater seal.

questions.q: Which strait separates Spain from Morocco?
questions.w: The Strait of Gibraltar, about 13 kilometres across at its narrowest.
questions.more: It is the only natural opening between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Around five million years ago it was closed, the Mediterranean largely dried out, and the refilling flood is thought to have been one of the largest in Earth's history.

questions.q: Which is the smallest country in the world by area?
questions.w: Vatican City, about 49 hectares, smaller than many city parks.
questions.more: Monaco is second at roughly four times the size. The Vatican has its own post office, railway platform and football team, and almost all of its citizens are clergy, so citizenship there usually ends when a job does.

questions.q: The Atacama, one of the driest places on Earth, is in which country?
questions.w: Chile. Parts of it have gone centuries without measurable rain.
questions.more: The Andes block moisture from the east and a cold ocean current kills it from the west. The sky is so clear and dry that many of the world's biggest telescopes are built there, and NASA tests Mars rovers on its soil.

questions.q: Mount Kilimanjaro is in which country?
questions.w: Tanzania, near the Kenyan border. At 5,895 metres it is Africa's highest point.
questions.more: It is a dormant volcano rather than part of a range, which is why it rises so abruptly from the plain. Its glaciers have shrunk by more than 80 per cent since 1912 and may be gone within decades.

questions.q: Select every South American country that is landlocked.
questions.w: Bolivia and Paraguay are the only two. Peru and Chile both have long Pacific coasts.
questions.more: Bolivia lost its coast to Chile in the War of the Pacific in 1879 and has never accepted it. It still maintains a navy, which patrols Lake Titicaca and the rivers, and marks a Day of the Sea every March.

questions.q: Put these capital cities in order from north to south.
questions.w: Oslo at about 60 degrees north, then Berlin at 52, Rome at 42 and Cairo at 30.
questions.more: Latitude is a poor guide to climate. Oslo sits further north than much of Canada's populated south, yet stays far milder because the North Atlantic current carries warm water up the Norwegian coast.

questions.q: Which African country was never brought under lasting European colonial rule?
questions.w: Ethiopia. Italy occupied it from 1936 to 1941 but never established colonial rule, and Ethiopian forces had beaten an earlier Italian invasion in 1896.
questions.more: That earlier victory, at Adwa, was a shock in Europe and made Ethiopia a symbol of independence across the continent and beyond. Liberia is the other country usually named, founded in the 1820s for freed American slaves.

questions.q: Which country has the longest coastline in the world?
questions.w: Canada, at over 200,000 kilometres, far ahead of anywhere else.
questions.more: Most of that length is the Arctic archipelago, tens of thousands of islands whose ragged edges add up. Coastline figures depend on how finely you measure, a problem known as the coastline paradox.

questions.q: The Danube passes through more countries than any other river. How many?
questions.w: Ten: Germany, Austria, Slovakia, Hungary, Croatia, Serbia, Romania, Bulgaria, Moldova and Ukraine.
questions.more: It also touches four capital cities, more than any other river: Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade. It rises in Germany's Black Forest and empties into the Black Sea.

questions.q: Which line of latitude runs through Australia, Chile and South Africa?
questions.w: The Tropic of Capricorn, at about 23.5 degrees south, the furthest south the sun is ever directly overhead.
questions.more: It is named for the constellation the sun sat in at the December solstice when the Greeks named it. Because Earth's tilt slowly shifts, the sun is now in Sagittarius at that moment and the line is creeping towards the Equator.
